Formalizing Lie Algebra Embeddings in Lean 4 — Scalability Lessons from E₈ (88 files, zero sorry)

Background & disclosure

Yeah, Im human

New to the community. I've been formalizing Lie algebra structures in Lean 4 with mathlib, and wanted to share what emerged — including some scalability lessons that may be useful to others working with large algebraic structures.

The repo name ("UFT") reflects a physics motivation: I started from Eric Dollard's electrical engineering work and built upward through standard Lie algebra embeddings to explore how far formal verification could take it. The physics interpretation is speculative and clearly marked as such. What I'm sharing here is the pure mathematics and the Lean engineering — the proofs stand regardless of the physics framing.
Disclosure: This work was done in collaboration with Claude (Anthropic). I'm an aviation electronics technician by background, currently pursuing an MFA in interactive design — I am not a mathematician. I used Claude throughout for proof strategy, mathlib API navigation, and code generation. Every proof compiles and is machine-verified, but I wanted to be transparent about that upfront.

What exists

  • 88 compiled proof files, ~2,975 declarations, zero sorry
  • Five certified LieHoms: three composing into a chain SU(5) →ₗ⁅ℝ⁆ SO(10) →ₗ⁅ℝ⁆ SO(14) →ₗ⁅ℝ⁆ SO(16), plus SO(4) →ₗ⁅ℝ⁆ SO(14) and a separate SO(14) →ₗ⁅ℝ⁆ SO(14)_matrix type bridge
  • E₈ as a 248-dimensional Lie algebra, verified via sparse Jacobi identity (7,752 nonzero brackets; native_decide over all 248³ triples)
  • SO(16) ⊂ E₈ subalgebra closure verified
  • Lie-Schur lemma and Killing form uniqueness (I couldn't find an existing formalization in Coq, Isabelle, or Mizar — corrections welcome)
  • Lean v4.29.0-rc4, mathlib dependency

The sparse Jacobi approach

Dense 248×248 matrix multiplication for the Jacobi check would be O(n⁵). Instead, we precompute only the nonzero structure constants (7,752 out of 248² = 61,504 possible) and verify the Jacobi identity via direct lookup — O(n⁴).

At dimension 50, the sparse approach was 88× faster than dense in our benchmarks. The 248³ ≈ 15.3M triples had to be chunked into 16 separate files to stay within compilation limits; each chunk handles a range of the first index and takes ~40 minutes to compile (parallelizable via lake build).

Scalability lessons (hitting Lean's limits with E₈)

Getting E₈ to compile taught us a lot about what Lean can and can't handle at scale:

  • Dense matrices failed first. The generated .lean files were too large; compilation ran out of memory.
  • Sparse representation was essential. Only the 7,752 nonzero structure constants, stored as a lookup function. This cut file size dramatically.
  • native_decide was required. decide alone couldn't handle the scale.
  • .olean files are enormous: SO(16) is 2.1 GB, SO(14) is 1.1 GB, SO(10) is 198 MB, E₈ sparse defs is 32 MB. Incremental compilation is not optional — a full rebuild is painful.
  • SageMath as oracle. Structure constants (Chevalley basis) were computed in SageMath and hard-coded into Lean for verification.

Patterns that might generalize
Type bridge pattern: We built Lie algebras by hand (flat structures with explicit brackets) and then proved LieHom into mathlib's matrix Lie algebra infrastructure. Useful for anyone constructing new Lie algebras that need to interface with mathlib's typeclass hierarchy.
Adding mathlib instances to hand-built algebras: A repeatable recipe for upgrading flat Lie algebra definitions to full LieRing + LieAlgebra ℝ instances. Tested on Bivector (6 gens), SL₃ (8), SL₅ (24), SU₅ (24), SO₁₀ (45), SO₁₄ (91), SO₁₆ (120). Pattern: define the bracket as a bilinear map, prove antisymmetry and Jacobi, then provide the instances. Happy to write this up more formally if there's interest.

Possible gaps in mathlib (corrections welcome)

  1. Lie-Schur lemma — a nonzero LieModuleHom between irreducible Lie modules is bijective. Mathlib has classical Schur for group representations; I couldn't find the Lie module version. Application: Killing form uniqueness (any invariant bilinear form on a simple Lie algebra is proportional to the Killing form).

  2. Antisymmetric trace identity — Tr(A{B,C}) = 0 for antisymmetric matrices A, B, C in any ring. Small standalone lemma, useful for anomaly computations in gauge theory.

Repo & key files

Repo: https://github.com/iarnoldy/UFT

Description

Jacobi chunks

Schur / Killing form

Type bridge

Antisymmetric trace identity

mathlib instance pattern

Happy to answer questions, share the SageMath oracle scripts, or extract pieces for potential mathlib PRs.
nah, im not a bot. i did, however, use claude for formatting.
I notice that many of your file paths mention clifford; is there a reason you avoided docs#CliffordAlgebra ?

thanks for pointing that out. it reflects the conceptual path through the project (which traces Clifford algebras Cl(1,1) → Cl(3,0) → Cl(1,3) → ...), but the actual Lean code doesn't use mathlib's CliffordAlgebra at all. Each Lie algebra is defined as a flat structure with explicit bracket tables, proiving LieRing + LieAlgebra ℝ instances directly. i want to be clear, im new to this, so thanks for going easy on me. not here to show off, just to collaborate
id be happy to convert it, that seems that it would be useful?

but the actual Lean code doesn't use mathlib's CliffordAlgebra at all

What I'm asking is what led you to make that choice?

the short and sweet is that I never attempted it in the first place. the project grew bottom-up starting by Cl(1,1) as a 4-element structure with an explicit multiplication table, then Cl(3,0) as 8 elements, then Cl(1,3) as 16 elements — each one hand-built with basis elements and verified products. By the time I reached the Lie algebra stage (SU(5), SO(10), etc.), the pattern was already "define a flat structure, write the bracket table, prove Jacobi." - kept going with what was working. if you look at the repo you can see that it started with the formalization of Dollards math in lean and then it just kept pointing upward

was reviewing my history and work and looking back, I think the reason we instinctively avoided it was scale. Cl(14) has 2^14 = 16,384 basis elements to extract 91 grade-2 generators, and Cl(16) has 65,536 elements for 120 generators. Our flat approach defines the Lie algebra directly at the grade-2 level and skips the exponential blowup entirely.

As far as I can tell, mathlib's CliffordAlgebra currently has no built-in connection to LieAlgebra — no grade-2 extraction, no commutator bracket construction.
I think probably the grade two extraction is around docs#CliffordAlgebra.even ?

Good looks! and fancy that, you wrote it! didnt even know that existed. It gives the even subalgebra (grades 0+2+4+...) which gets much closer than I thought. For Cl(1,3), the even part is 8-dimensional (1+6+1), and extracting the 6-dimensional grade-2 part (the bivectors = so(1,3)) from there seems very doable.

Did some research and it appears that for the small cases (Cl(1,1), Cl(1,3)), it seems to make sense to connect CliffordAlgebra.even → grade-2 projection → commutator bracket → LieRing instance. That would give a proper derivation of so(1,3) from the Clifford algebra rather than hand-defining the brackets.

For the larger algebras (so(14) with 91 generators, so(16) with 120), the even subalgebra of Cl(14) is 8,192-dimensional, which might hit the same compilation limits we ran into with the dense E₈ approach. Our flat hand-defined brackets seem more practical at that scale. It seems evident that the small-case construction would be a useful pattern for anyone building Lie algebras from Clifford algebras in Lean?

Would a PR constructing so(p,q) as grade-2 of CliffordAlgebra.even (for small p+q) be useful to mathlib?

Not if it is written by AI, no, because AI cannot write code at a sufficiently high quality to make it worth reviewing, at this point in time.

See https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/index.html#use-of-ai

I'm afraid I don't have the time to look at this repo but I will add some remarks about my thoughts in this direction.

Ultimately I think that we should have (at least) two constructions of the E8E_8E8​ Lie algebra. The first should be useful for proving abstract results and the second should be useful for doing concrete calculations within the Lie algebra itself. (This pattern is common to many mathematical objects including the natural numbers where Peano's axioms are great for proving but for computation we want a representation using binary expansions.)

For the first (for abstract results) we already have docs#RootPairing.GeckConstruction.lieAlgebra which reduces the problem of constructing the Lie algebra to the much easier problem of constructing the E8E_8E8​ root system. Furthermore once we merge #34727 we will know a lot about this Lie algebra. We also have the Serre construction implemented as docs#LieAlgebra.e₈ but we have proved nothing about this.

For the second (for concrete calculations) we should indeed have a giant concrete Chevalley basis somewhere (which is possibly what you've got) together with a proof that it is equivalent to the abstract definition(s).

Somewhat related to both of these is the PR #36298

In theory there is a lovely body of work to do here: Lie algebras and their representations have some very nice algorithmic properties (presumably all implemented in SageMath) and with sufficient work we could formally verify all of these.

Hopefully these remarks give some idea of the sorts of code and results we are looking for in Mathlib.

first piece: bivectors in a Clifford algebra form a LieSubalgebra under the commutator bracket. 345 lines, zero sorry, compiles clean against current mathlib. Three imports (CliffordAlgebra.Grading, Lie.OfAssociative, Tactic.NoncommRing).

It defines CliffordAlgebra.bivector (the Submodule spanned by ι m₁ * ι m₂), proves the explicit commutator formula, proves bracket closure via span_induction₂, and packages it as CliffordAlgebra.bivectorLieSubalgebra. Also connects to the grading via bivector_le_evenOdd_zero. Maximum generality — CommRing R, AddCommGroup M, Module R M.

Full disclosure: this was built entirely with AI assistance (Claude). I'm not a Lean programmer — my background is aviation electronics. I directed the construction and QA process so I cant maintain it through API changes. I'm not fooling myself, I'm not the right person to submit the PR.

If anyone wants to champion it, the file is yours. A few things a reviewer should look at:

  1. The commutator expansion proofs use noncomm_ring for associativity steps. I know mathlib's CliffordAlgebra files prefer direct rw chains with mul_assoc/sub_mul — a champion would probably want to clean that up.
  2. LieModule R (CliffordAlgebra Q) (CliffordAlgebra Q) doesn't synthesize automatically — exceeds the heartbeat limit. I worked around it with an explicit instance. Might warrant an upstream issue.
  3. My research shows the natural follow-up would be a LieEquiv connecting this to skewAdjointMatricesLieSubalgebra for finite-dimensional cases.

real quick - I reworked it based on your feedback. The updated version:

- Generalized to nvector n Q (grade-n submodule, spanned by n-fold products of ι), with bivector Q := nvector Q 2
- Replaced all rw [show with direct rw chains using mul_assoc/sub_mul/Algebra.commutes + abel to close
- Dropped the NoncommRing import entirely

A few questions came up during the rework:

1. The spanning set for nvector 2 Q includes ι m * ι m = Q(m), so the submodule contains scalars — not just pure grade-2 elements. The Lie subalgebra result still holds (scalars commute trivially), but should the definition be tightened to exclude the scalar part?
2. On naming: I used nvector but I see mathlib uses exteriorPower for the analogous concept in ExteriorAlgebra (defined as (LinearMap.range ι) ^ n). That same pattern would have the same filtration issue here. Is there a better name or definition you'd prefer for the Clifford case?

Updated gist: https://gist.github.com/iarnoldy/a2a90a145eba19b74f62ee0f92fbf7b9

. On naming: I used nvector but I see mathlib uses exteriorPower for the analogous concept in ExteriorAlgebra (defined as (LinearMap.range ι) ^ n). That same pattern would have the same filtration issue here

You can avoid the filtration issue by pulling back exteriorPower into the clifford algebra along the canonical equivalence. Of course, then you'll realize you need to not be in characteristic two!

Got it — pull back exteriorPower through equivExterior for pure grades. I see CliffordAlgebra.equivExterior exists in Contraction.lean with [Invertible (2 : R)]. So the definition would be something like (exteriorPower R 2 M).map (equivExterior Q).symm. The char-2 restriction is fine for the Lie subalgebra use case.
